title: Reading News
intro: Two fortieth birthdays this issue — Mrs Large's bath and the Oxford Reading Tree — plus Michael Morpurgo's memoir arriving on Thursday, twenty-five years of the Roman Mysteries, and the first sign that reading enjoyment has stopped falling.

items.headline: Five Minutes' Peace turns forty, and Mrs Large still doesn't get any
items.author: Jill Murphy
items.book: A Bad Spell for the Worst Witch
items.summary: The Worst Witch is still the most-read series across our schools, but Murphy's other great creation had its fortieth birthday this year. Walker Books published Five Minutes' Peace in 1986, and Mrs Large has been trying to eat her breakfast in the bath ever since. It is the surest laugh in a Reception read-aloud, and it pairs neatly with the Worst Witch if you want one author to carry a whole-school week rather than two.

items.headline: Forty years of Biff, Chip and Kipper, and Oxford is marking it
items.author: Roderick Hunt
items.summary: Roderick Hunt and illustrator Alex Brychta created Biff, Chip, Kipper and Floppy in 1986, so 2026 is the Oxford Reading Tree's fortieth year. Oxford University Press puts the reach at more than 30 million children across over 130 countries. Nearly everything our schools log is the early levels, where the magic key first turns up, and Oxford Owl's free ebook library is the easy thing to point parents at for home reading.

items.headline: Morpurgo's memoir is out on Thursday, and the farm behind it turns fifty
items.author: Michael Morpurgo
items.summary: Down Burrow Lane is Morpurgo's account of the remote Devon farm he and Clare moved to as a young schoolteacher and his wife — the one that gave him War Horse, Private Peaceful and Farm Boy. Hodder & Stoughton publish it on 17 September. Farms for City Children, the charity that farm became, was founded in 1976 and so turns fifty this year, with more than 100,000 children having stayed on its farms since.

items.headline: Twenty-five years of the Roman Mysteries, and seventeen books to work through
items.author: Caroline Lawrence
items.summary: The Thieves of Ostia, the first of the Roman Mysteries, was published in 2001, which makes the series twenty-five this year. The Enemies of Jupiter, the one our schools read most, is book seven of seventeen — so a child who has just finished it has ten more ahead of them. The BBC televised the series in 2007 and 2008 if you want Flavia's Ostia in pictures as well as in print.

events.name: Julia Donaldson's birthday
events.blurb: Born 16 September 1948, and still the safest bet in any infant classroom. It falls on the Wednesday this year, which is a gift if you want a mid-week story session that needs no preparation.

events.name: National Poetry Day
events.blurb: Thursday 1 October, and this year's theme is wonder. The National Literacy Trust has free classroom resources ready to download if you would rather not build something from scratch.

events.name: Michael Morpurgo's birthday
events.blurb: Born 5 October 1943, so he turns 83 a fortnight after Down Burrow Lane comes out. A neat excuse to put War Horse or Farm Boy in front of an upper key stage 2 class.

events.name: National Non-Fiction November
events.blurb: The whole of November, run by the Federation of Children's Book Groups. The child who will not touch a story but knows every fact about sharks gets a month where that counts as reading. This year's theme had not been announced when we went to press.

events.name: First Children's Booker Prize shortlist
events.blurb: Tuesday 24 November, when the eight shortlisted books are named along with the three children aged 8 to 12 who will judge alongside the adults. Eight titles aimed squarely at your upper key stage 2 readers, arriving just in time for the spring term.

general.label: Reading research
general.text: Reading enjoyment has gone up for the first time in five years. The National Literacy Trust's 2026 annual survey, taken by 125,375 children and young people between January and March, found 36.1% of 8 to 18-year-olds enjoy reading in their free time — a small rise from the lowest figure since the survey began in 2005.

general.label: Worth knowing
general.text: BookTrust's Bookbuzz Primary lets every child in Years 3 to 6 choose a book from sixteen hand-picked titles and keep it. It costs £3.65 a pupil, the school also gets two copies of each of the sixteen for its own shelves, and registration for 2026 is open.

general.label: Worth knowing
general.text: Registration for the 2027 Yoto Carnegies shadowing scheme opens in November. Longlists are announced in February and shortlists in March, with the winners in late June — and longlist shadowing is age-inclusive, so a primary reading group can take part rather than only secondary ones.

general.label: Reading news
general.text: The Booker Prize Foundation has launched a Children's Booker Prize for fiction aimed at 8 to 12-year-olds. The winner takes £50,000, the shortlist of eight is announced on 24 November 2026, and the winner on 2 February 2027 — chosen by a panel that includes three children.
